content: Proper precautions are critical during the transportation of antidotes and antivenoms, from the point of importation to local storage facilities and transitional storage areas. Efforts should be directed toward developing antidotes and antivenoms with extended shelf lives and improved stability under extreme conditions, such as high temperatures and humidity, particularly for regions where maintaining proper storage conditions is challenging. Poison centers play a pivotal role in national antidote programs. They are uniquely positioned to provide a comprehensive overview of poisoning patterns within their region or country. This enables them to identify the specific antidotes required for their area and analyze data to localize poisoning cases. Their role becomes even more significant in settings where hospital documentation and reporting of poisoning cases are inadequate. However, even the most effective antidote will be of limited use if the attending physician cannot make an accurate diagnosis or is unaware of the antidote's availability or indications for use. Poison centers should actively educate clinical personnel on the appropriate use of antidotes and antivenoms and ideally organize training programs to enhance the diagnosis and management of poisoning cases. As centers of expertise in clinical toxicology, poison centers should critically review and evaluate the scientific literature on antidote effectiveness and provide informed advice to relevant authorities regarding decisions on antidote registration and procurement. They should also promote the establishment of a national network for antidote supply, requiring close collaboration with responsible authorities and hospital pharmacies. Additionally, poison centers can participate in international information exchanges to assess the efficacy and safety of antidotal agents. These assessments should be based on internationally standardized data collection to facilitate result comparisons. Since the data available at the time of certain antidotes' registration may have been limited, it is essential to update this information with more recent findings. Poison centers should also gather data on medicinal products used for other indications that have proven effective in treating poisoning. Animal poisoning is a significant issue in many parts of the world, and poison centers frequently receive inquiries about its treatment. The use of antidotes in veterinary medicine presents challenges related to selection, dosage, administration routes, and availability. Each country should establish a working group with expertise in veterinary toxicology, including poison specialists, veterinarians, and regulatory authorities, to address these issues. In some countries, off-label use of human drugs for animals is permitted, such as under the Animal Medicinal Drug Use Clarification Act of 1994 in the USA, which allows veterinarians to prescribe human or veterinary drugs for off-label purposes, with liability resting on the prescribing veterinarian. Veterinary prescribing also raises concerns about the potential entry of medicines or antidotes into the food chain, necessitating adherence to appropriate withdrawal period guidelines. Including relevant antidotes and antivenoms in the national essential medicines list or formulary is crucial to allocate resources for their procurement and distribution through public health services. Mechanisms should be established for the rapid importation of antidotes for emergency use, and special arrangements may be needed for the controlled clinical use of antidotes still under development. The WHO initiative for assessing and listing snake antivenoms aims to improve access to antivenoms of acceptable quality, safety, and efficacy. National health authorities should encourage the local manufacture and distribution of unavailable antidotes, potentially providing incentives to pharmaceutical manufacturers, hospital pharmacies, and service laboratories. Exportation of these antidotes could also be promoted. At the international level, establishing a mechanism for the global purchase, storage, and distribution of certain antidotes could address availability issues in some countries, though this would require significant economic resources and political commitment. Regional cooperative groups for antidote supply and storage could overcome many obstacles, fostering collaboration among international organizations, poison centers, and toxicological associations. For example, the WHO South-East Asia Region has initiated a pilot project for coordinated antidote procurement, with distribution managed by Thailand's Ministry of Health and emergency provision facilitated by the Ramathibodi Poison Center in Bangkok. High-income countries could support lowand middle-income countries by sharing resources and expertise through development assistance programs, facilitating the establishment of antidote storage depots and improving the management of poisoned patients. In suitable hospital pharmacy facilities in lowand middle-income countries, some antidotes could be prepared locally in cooperation with poison centers, provided quality assurance processes are in place. Education grants and training courses for pharmaceutical staff in this area would be valuable and could be encouraged through international exchange programs to develop human resources. Poison centers are encouraged to maintain comprehensive records of inquiries and poisoning cases, which are essential for medico-legal, audit, and administrative purposes. Systematic data collection supports toxicovigilance, epidemiological studies, quality assurance, and the development of treatment protocols. Annual reports summarizing poisoning data, workload, and activities provide valuable insights into poisoning patterns and support discussions with funders.
